title: Community college transfer students lose degree-applicable credits because articulation rules are fragmented, year-specific, and evaluated course-by-course after admission
affected_user: Community college students transferring to four-year universities (especially CA CCC->UC/CSU, Texas public 2-year->4-year); secondarily community college transfer counselors and university articulation officers
job_to_be_done: Know before enrolling in a course whether it will count toward a specific major and GE requirement at the target university, and get the credit honored on arrival
current_process: Student checks ASSIST.org (CA) or a receiving school's catalog; agreements are keyed to the year the course was taken, split across department vs. GE/Breadth tabs, and courses joined by '&' must be taken as a set. Where no articulation agreement exists, each course is reviewed individually by the receiving school, usually after admission or after an official transcript evaluation. Texas caps accepted transfer at 66 hours, with the rest downgraded to electives.
what_fails: Credits transfer as electives rather than toward the major/GE; agreement-year mismatches cause denials; students transferring before completing an associate degree lose articulation guarantees; the fine print (minimum grades, time limits, lower-division caps, residency) is discovered too late.
failure_frequency: GAO-17-574 (2017): transferring students lost an estimated 43% of credits on average (2004-2009 cohort), ~22% for public 2-yr to public 4-yr path; CUNY Office of Policy Research (2022) found 47% of ~5,700 vertical transfer students lost degree-applicable credits; Inside Higher Ed (Jan 2026) cites 58% of adults who tried to transfer credit losing some.
cost_of_failure: Lost credits typically force an extra semester of tuition and delay; GAO linked credit loss to lower six-year bachelor's completion. Dollar figure per student not found in a primary source.
existing_workaround: Students ask the receiving school for a written credit evaluation, hoard syllabi to petition course-by-course, retake courses, or delay transfer until the ADT/associate degree is complete; counselors manually cross-reference ASSIST agreements by year.
who_pays_today: Students (extra tuition, time, lost Pell eligibility); state systems fund ASSIST.org and articulation officer staff; third-party guides (Edvisorly, Transfermatic, TransferCredit.org) monetize the confusion.

sources.note: GAO estimated transferring students lost ~43% of credits on average; students receive limited information about articulation.
Cites CUNY 2022 study: 47% of 5,700 vertical transfer students lost degree-applicable credits.
Nearly 4 in 10 adults have tried to transfer credit; 58% of those lost credits.
Texas reporting on transfer credit loss; 66-hour cap with excess becoming electives (only snippet seen).
Berkeley advising: credit reviewed per the ASSIST agreement for the year the course was taken; GE vs department tabs differ; '&'-joined courses cannot be split.
Lists common traps: grade cutoffs, course age limits, residency, lower-division caps, elective-only transfer.

firsthand_evidence: No Reddit/forum firsthand threads surfaced in search results (r/CollegeTransfer queries returned only guides and official pages). Firsthand pain is INFERRED from the volume of 'how to avoid losing credits' guides and GAO's finding that students get inadequate information.
key_unknowns: Current (post-2020) national credit-loss rate; how much of CA ADT/ASSIST loss is at the GE vs. major level; whether receiving institutions' evaluation data (course equivalency tables) is accessible without institutional access; what share of loss is due to student information gaps vs. institutional refusal.
technical_unlock: ASSIST.org and many university equivalency tables are public and scrapable (Playwright); LLM parsing of syllabi against course outlines for equivalency pre-checks; per-year agreement diffing to warn students of agreement changes before they enroll.
why_now: Jan 2026 and Mar 2026 press coverage shows renewed policy attention (Texas, national 'learning mobility' agenda); states adding transfer mandates; AI course-equivalency research (Berkeley 2019 machine-translation articulation paper) shows the equivalency problem is tractable.
existing_solutions: ASSIST.org (CA), Transferology, Edvisorly, Transfermatic, TransferCredit.org, CollegeSource TES (institutional), state articulation portals (FL).

title: 2026-27 FAFSA verification and new real-time identity/fraud screening hold aid for weeks to months, with processing pauses and glitches at the federal level
affected_user: College students (especially first-generation and low-income) selected for verification or identity checks; campus financial aid offices processing them
job_to_be_done: Get a final aid offer and disbursement before tuition deadlines and the start of term
current_process: Student files FAFSA; FSA runs fraud/identity screening (real-time since ~April 2026; a one-time batch screen placed ~300,000 2026-27 forms in Verification Tracking Group V5). School is notified 3-5 weeks after filing; student uploads tax transcripts, W-2s, ID/statement of educational purpose; aid office reviews in 2-3 weeks per school; offers are not final and nothing disburses until verification is complete.
what_fails: Federal processing of FAFSA updates was paused (CSUN: updates on/after April 26, 2026 not processed until system fixes late June, campus processing resuming late July); a June 29-July 6, 2026 glitch dropped fraud-screening results from some forms; selected students wait through multiple sequential 2-3 week queues; aid offices face higher volume in a shorter window after the Sept 24, 2025 early launch.
failure_frequency: ~300,000 2026-27 applications selected for V5 identity verification by the one-time batch screen (FSA, Aug 2026); financial verification selection rate estimates conflict (5% vs. ~one-third of filers); per-school processing 2-3 weeks after documents, plus 3-5 week notification lag (U. Arizona).
cost_of_failure: Aid not disbursed until verification complete (Georgia Tech policy page); students miss tuition deadlines or defer enrollment; staff time in aid offices. No primary dollar estimate found.
existing_workaround: Students call aid offices early in the week, check studentaid.gov repeatedly, pay deposits out of pocket or take emergency loans; schools post 'temporary delay' notices; consultant/blog guides sell 'clear verification fast' advice.
who_pays_today: Students (delayed/forfeited aid, late fees); institutions (aid office staffing, Ellucian/other SIS vendors); FSA contractors.

sources.note: FSA: one-time fraud screening of pre-real-time 2026-27 forms completed; ~300,000 applications selected for V5 verification.
CSUN notice: FAFSA updates submitted on/after April 26, 2026 paused; federal system updates late June, campus processing resumes ~late July.
2026-27 FAFSA launched Sept 24, 2025; aid offices face higher volume in shorter window.
School is notified of selection 3-5 weeks after filing; review takes up to 3 weeks after all documents received.
Aid offers not final and not disbursed until verification complete.
Describes 2026 real-time identity check (4 risk tiers) and June 29-July 6 2026 glitch; secondary source, unconfirmed.

firsthand_evidence: No r/financialaid threads surfaced in results. Firsthand pain is inferred from institutional 'temporary delay' notices and FSA's own announcement of a 300,000-form verification batch.
key_unknowns: Actual median days from selection to disbursement in 2026-27; how many students abandon enrollment due to verification ('verification melt') this cycle; whether the delays are transient (one-time batch) or structural (real-time screening tiers); exact financial-verification selection rate.
technical_unlock: Document-checklist and status-tracking workflows per tracking group (V1/V4/V5) are rule-based and public in the FSA Application and Verification Guide; OCR/LLM pre-validation of uploaded tax transcripts and IDs could cut back-and-forth. Payer would be institutions, who already buy aid-office software.
why_now: Real-time FAFSA fraud detection introduced April 2026; one-time 300,000-form V5 batch in summer 2026; federal processing pause in spring/summer 2026; early (Sept) launch compresses timelines.
existing_solutions: Ellucian, Jenzabar, CampusLogic/Anthology StudentForms (verification workflow), ProVerifier, FSA's studentaid.gov status pages, consumer guides (CollegeLens, UsaDemia).

title: Special education teachers spend 10-20 unpaid hours a week on IEP paperwork and case management, driving attrition and vacancies that feed back into heavier caseloads
affected_user: K-12 special education teachers/case managers; secondarily parents waiting on evaluations and IEP meetings, and district SPED directors covering vacancies
job_to_be_done: Produce compliant, individualized IEPs, progress reports, evaluation reports, and meeting documentation on legal timelines while still teaching
current_process: Teachers draft IEPs in district IEP systems, gather assessment data, schedule and hold meetings, write present-levels and goals, log service minutes and progress, and respond to state compliance audits, mostly outside contracted hours; some districts hire dedicated paperwork staff or request caseload waivers above state limits (CA limit 28).
what_fails: Paperwork crowds out instruction; teachers copy/paste IEP text under caseload pressure (lower plan quality); timelines slip (state complaint decisions cite missed meetings and insufficient staffing); experienced teachers leave the field citing paperwork.
failure_frequency: BU researcher Bettini: ~10 hours/week outside school day, largely paperwork/case management; Minnesota legislative testimony: 15-20 unpaid hours/week; New Ulm district estimate 32-61 hours per student per year, 480-915 hours at a 15-student caseload; NCES: ~70% of public schools reported SPED teacher vacancies in 2023-24.
cost_of_failure: Teacher attrition (Teach Plus IL 2023: paperwork among main reasons former SPED teachers left); districts hire paperwork staff (Philadelphia example) or pay compliance consultants and due-process legal costs; students lose services (Maine due-process decision cites staffing shortfalls).
existing_workaround: Unpaid overtime; reusing/boilerplating IEP text; districts hiring IEP paperwork clerks; teachers using general-purpose AI to draft IEPs (EdWeek Oct 2025), which advocates say raises privacy/individualization concerns.
who_pays_today: Districts (IEP software licenses, compliance staff, legal fees), teachers (unpaid time), states (monitoring), and families (advocates/attorneys).

sources.note: Teachers describe crushing paperwork; a Philadelphia teacher's school hired staff to handle IEP paperwork.
Former Illinois SPED teachers cite IEP paperwork as a main reason for leaving.
Teachers using AI to draft IEPs; Bettini estimate ~10 extra hours/week; 70% of schools had SPED vacancies (NCES 2023-24).
Minnesota legislative document: 15-20 unpaid hours/week; district estimate 32-61 hours per student.
North Dakota survey to lawmakers: SPED staff report burnout and uncompensated work time.
Due-process decision records district citing insufficient staffing for missed services.

firsthand_evidence: WVIA (Oct 26, 2026): a Philadelphia special educator said the biggest struggle was juggling IEP paperwork with teaching until his school hired dedicated paperwork staff. No r/specialed threads surfaced in results, though the pattern is corroborated by Teach Plus interviews and ND survey testimony.
key_unknowns: Which specific documents consume the most hours (present levels vs. progress monitoring vs. meeting notes); how locked-in districts are to incumbent IEP platforms (Frontline/SEIS/PowerSchool); FERPA/IDEA constraints on any third-party drafting tool; whether districts will pay for teacher-side tools vs. only district-side compliance tools.
technical_unlock: Structured extraction from assessment reports into present-levels and goal drafts; progress-monitoring data capture that auto-generates quarterly progress reports; timeline/compliance calendaring. Caveat: the brief deprioritizes pure LLM wrappers; the durable piece is the workflow/data capture, not drafting.
why_now: Oct 2025-Oct 2026 coverage shows teachers already using AI for IEPs ad hoc; vacancy rates near 70% of schools; state legislatures (MN, ND) taking testimony on SPED workload in 2026.
existing_solutions: Frontline IEP, PowerSchool Special Programs, SEIS (CA), Embrace, Magic School / Brisk / general LLMs for drafting, Govtech-covered AI IEP tools.

title: OPT/STEM OPT adjudication delays in 2026 leave F-1 graduates unable to start jobs, burning unemployment days and job offers
affected_user: F-1 international students and recent graduates applying for post-completion OPT or the 24-month STEM extension; university DSOs/ISSS offices; employers with pending hires
job_to_be_done: Receive an EAD and start work within the narrow window between graduation, the 14-month OPT completion rule, and the 90/150-day unemployment limits
current_process: DSO issues recommendation in SEVIS (60-day clock to file); student files I-765 (standard or $1,780 premium since March 1, 2026); SEVIS unemployment counter starts on the approved start date even if the card arrives later; STEM extension filed up to 90 days before EAD expiry.
what_fails: Standard processing reported at 3-5 months with some 6-12+ month cases in 2026; roughly 12,000 students reported stuck in stalled OPT/STEM OPT adjudications in early 2026; a pending initial OPT does not authorize work, so the usable OPT period shrinks; unemployment days accrue between approval and card receipt; employment-update lapses in SEVP Portal trigger status warnings.
failure_frequency: ~12,000 students in stalled adjudications (VisaVerge, early 2026); processing 90-120 days typical with 6+ month delays reported (scale.jobs 2026); premium processing fee $1,780 (VisaVerge).
cost_of_failure: Lost or rescinded job offers; up to $1,780 premium fee per filing to buy certainty; months of foregone salary; risk of status loss when unemployment limits (90 days post-completion, 150 cumulative on STEM) are exceeded.
existing_workaround: Pay premium processing; universities (Cornell, MIT/ACE) send letters to DHS/USCIS; students track SEVIS counters manually and consult DSOs; forum advice (Teamblind) to contact the school's SEVIS contact when employment updates are missed.
who_pays_today: Students (premium fees, lost wages), universities (ISSS staff), employers (delayed starts), immigration law firms.

sources.note: Reports ~12,000 students frozen in stalled OPT/STEM OPT adjudications in 2026.
Premium processing fee rose to $1,780 for filings postmarked on/after March 1, 2026; delays endanger job offers.
Law firm: slow initial OPT decisions shorten usable OPT under the 14-month rule.
Typical 90-120 days; six-month-plus delays reported in early 2026.
Cornell letter to DHS on OPT processing delays (institutional complaint).
Student missed an SEVP employment update and received an unemployment-days-exhausted warning.
SEVIS unemployment counter rules (days allowed/accrued/remaining).

firsthand_evidence: Teamblind post: a student forgot to update employment in the SEVP portal and got a warning that unemployment days were exhausted; commenters told them to go through the school's SEVIS contact. No Reddit threads appeared in results.
key_unknowns: Official USCIS I-765 (c)(3) processing-time data for 2026 (not retrieved); whether the court-enjoined Sept 2026 DHS rule will reinstate; share of students who lose offers vs. merely delay; whether DSOs would adopt third-party tracking tools given SEVIS access rules.
technical_unlock: Deadline/unemployment-day tracking across SEVIS rules, I-765 timelines and employer updates is deterministic and could be built from public rules; aggregate self-reported case timelines (like trackitt-style) could give students real processing estimates. No privileged access needed for a student-side tool.
why_now: 2026 backlog (~12,000 cases), premium fee hike March 2026, DHS rule enjoined Sept 14, 2026, and heightened SEVIS scrutiny since 2025.
existing_solutions: USCIS premium processing, university ISSS pages, law-firm blogs, Zolve timelines, informal trackers on Reddit/Blind/trackitt.

title: Adult ESL and literacy programs have long waitlists that grew in 2026 as federal refugee/adult-ed funding was cut
affected_user: Adult immigrants and refugees seeking English classes; community literacy nonprofits, libraries, and community college noncredit ESL departments
job_to_be_done: Get into a beginner/intermediate English class within weeks of arrival so the learner can work, navigate services, and pursue a GED or credential
current_process: Learner registers with a nonprofit, library, or community college; when sections fill, the provider opens a waitlist (sometimes closed outright); volunteers and small staff manage intake, placement testing, and waitlists by hand; funding comes from WIOA Title II, refugee resettlement grants, and donations.
what_fails: Capacity collapses when grants are cut (Literacy Green Bay cut from 15 classes to 8 and has a ~300-person waitlist after federal refugee funding changes, Sept 2026); libraries close their waitlists (Round Rock, TX); community college ESL sections run full with waitlists (Cuesta College Spring 2026); learners wait months to years (UK example: up to 2 years).
failure_frequency: Green Bay: ~300 on waitlist for one provider (2026-09); Cuesta College Spring 2026 waitlist report shows ESL sections with 1-17 waiting; ERIC 'ESL Logjam' documents long waits in many regions (older, undated in results).
cost_of_failure: Delayed workforce entry and earnings for learners; lost grant deliverables and donor confidence for providers; no primary dollar estimate found.
existing_workaround: Closed waitlists, volunteer-led conversation groups, library self-study, commercial apps, learners traveling to neighboring providers; providers fundraising to replace lost federal grants.
who_pays_today: Federal (WIOA Title II, refugee resettlement), states, local libraries, donors; learners pay with time and delayed employment.

sources.note: Literacy Green Bay cut ESL classes from 15 to 8 after federal funding losses; ~300-person waitlist.
Same story republished by PBS Wisconsin (deduplicated).
Library ESL waitlist closed; will reopen later.
Spring 2026 waitlisted-classes report shows ESL sections with waiting students at full capacity.
'The ESL Logjam': long waiting lists for adult ESL in many parts of the US (older report).
UK comparison: two-year waits, lists of up to 400 per course (structural, non-US).

firsthand_evidence: Provider staff in Green Bay (Sept 2026) describe hundreds of immigrants and refugees waiting after classes were cut; no learner-authored forum posts surfaced.
key_unknowns: National 2026 adult-ed waitlist totals (no NRS/OCTAE figure found); whether the bottleneck is funding (teachers/space) or administrative (intake, placement, scheduling); willingness of small nonprofits to pay for any software; whether 2026 federal cuts are permanent.
technical_unlock: Low-cost waitlist/intake/placement coordination across providers in a region; asynchronous, teacher-light instruction to bridge the wait. Note: capacity loss from funding cuts is not a software problem; only the coordination/bridging piece is addressable.
why_now: 2026 federal refugee resettlement and adult-ed funding cuts (per Green Bay reporting) shrinking supply while demand persists.
existing_solutions: ProLiteracy networks, Burlington English, USA Learns, Duolingo, library conversation circles, community college noncredit ESL.

title: Roughly one in five teacher absences goes unfilled by substitutes, forcing teachers to cover classes and schools to split or combine classrooms
affected_user: K-12 building administrators and HR/sub coordinators; classroom teachers who lose prep periods to cover; students in disadvantaged schools hit hardest
job_to_be_done: Fill every teacher absence with a qualified substitute by the start of the school day
current_process: Teachers enter absences in an absence-management system (e.g., Frontline); subs accept jobs from a pool; unfilled jobs are covered in-house by pulling teachers from prep periods, paraprofessionals, or administrators, or by combining classes.
what_fails: Sub pools are too thin; fill rates vary widely by district (one WI district 95% over Aug 2025-Feb 2026 with 71 of 1,439 jobs covered in-house; one MO district improved from 70% in 2022-23 to 99% in 2025-26); Illinois districts cover 16,500+ absences/week with ~20% unfilled; nationally ~1 in 5 requests went unfilled pre-pandemic with 77% of districts reporting worse conditions after.
failure_frequency: Illinois survey (~400 districts): 16,500+ absences/week, ~20% unfilled (date not confirmed); Future-Ed: 1 in 5 requests unfilled pre-pandemic (undated); Kimberly, WI board report: ~5% unfilled Aug 2025-Feb 2026.
cost_of_failure: Lost teacher prep time, paid coverage stipends, lost instruction; 37,569 unfilled teaching positions across 29 states + DC (LPI 2026) compound the problem. Dollar figures not found in results.
existing_workaround: Teacher coverage stipends, combining classes, raising sub pay, lowering sub credential requirements, outsourcing to staffing firms (Kelly, ESS, Swing), in-house 'building sub' positions.
who_pays_today: Districts (sub pay, staffing agencies, Frontline absence-management licenses, coverage stipends); teachers (lost prep time).

sources.note: Illinois survey of ~400 districts: 16,500+ absences/week, ~20% unfilled.
Vendor analysis of fill rates across its absence-management data.
Annenberg (Brown) research: sub shortage hits disadvantaged schools hardest.
One WI district: 95.07% fill rate, 71 of 1,439 jobs covered in-house, Aug 2025-Feb 2026.
37,569 unfilled teaching positions across 29 states + DC.
Reports Future-Ed finding: 1 in 5 sub requests unfilled pre-pandemic; 77% of districts worse after.

firsthand_evidence: None found in results (r/Teachers threads did not surface); evidence is district board reports and surveys.
key_unknowns: A national 2026 unfilled-rate statistic (not found); whether the constraint is sub supply (pay/credentialing) or matching/scheduling inefficiency; incumbent lock-in to Frontline/Red Rover/SmartFind; whether small districts without absence-management software exist in meaningful numbers.
technical_unlock: Better sub-matching (notification timing, teacher-preferred sub lists, geographic routing) is a standard marketplace problem; district-level fill-rate analytics from existing exports. Payer is districts; sales cycles are long.
why_now: Post-ESSER budget cliffs and 2026 teacher vacancy data (LPI) keep pressure on coverage; some districts report recovery (99% fill), so the problem is uneven.
existing_solutions: Frontline Absence Management, Red Rover, SmartFind Express, Swing Education, Kelly Education, ESS, Scoot.

title: Chronic-absenteeism interventions are run as manual, threshold-triggered letter workflows that reach families late and are hard to track across tiers
affected_user: School attendance clerks, counselors, and assistant principals; district attendance/MTSS coordinators; families of chronically absent students
job_to_be_done: Identify students approaching the 10% chronic-absence threshold early, contact families in the right channel and language by the 3rd absence, document every contact for state compliance, and escalate through tiers
current_process: Attendance recorded in the SIS; district policy triggers letters at fixed counts (e.g., 5/10/15 absences, Rahway NJ 2025-26 plan) with monthly data reviews; staff mail letters, make calls, and log contacts; state toolkits (KY) and Attendance Works provide letter templates; California SB 691 pushes earlier contact.
what_fails: Letters go out after students are already chronically absent; multi-channel follow-up (mail + text) and the 2-3 week follow-up recommended by evidence-based 'nudge letter' models are not systematically scheduled; documentation for state notices and truancy referrals is scattered across SIS, email, and spreadsheets.
failure_frequency: Threshold letters fire at 5/10/15 absences per district policy; EdSource/SB 691 commentary says contact should happen by the 3rd absence. National 2025-26 chronic absence rate not retrieved in this session (search budget exhausted).
cost_of_failure: Lost instruction and state attendance-based funding (CA ADA funding); staff hours mailing and logging; vendor claims (unverified) that early outreach cuts chronic absence 45% imply large avoidable loss.
existing_workaround: Paper/mail-merge letters from SIS, Attendance Works templates, state toolkits, vendor nudge-letter services (SchoolStatus, Panorama), monthly attendance team meetings.
who_pays_today: Districts (SchoolStatus/Panorama/EveryDay Labs contracts, postage, clerk time); states fund attendance initiatives; families bear truancy consequences.

sources.note: FutureEd 2026 Attendance Playbook: tiered, evidence-based attendance interventions (only fragments visible).
Commentary on CA SB 691: reach families by the 3rd absence; over half improve without second intervention.
Vendor: hybrid mailed + digital letters recommended; 54% never need a second intervention (vendor data).
District plan: letters at 5/10/15 absences from the SIS with monthly data review (concrete manual workflow).
Nudge-letter model: brief letters/texts with follow-up 2-3 weeks later.
State DOE provides customizable letter templates, implying districts assemble workflows themselves.

firsthand_evidence: None found; evidence is policy documents, a district plan, and vendor/commentary sources. No staff complaint posts surfaced.
key_unknowns: How many districts lack a vendor nudge-letter contract; whether the bottleneck is workflow tooling or family-level causes (health, transportation) that letters cannot fix; current national chronic-absence rate; SIS integration access for a small vendor.
technical_unlock: SIS exports (CSV/OneRoster) plus rules engine for early, multilingual, multi-channel outreach with scheduled follow-ups and an audit log; cheap compared to enterprise vendors. Needs district buy-in and student-data agreements.
why_now: FutureEd Oct 2026 playbook and California SB 691 (2026) raise the bar for early, documented outreach; post-pandemic chronic absence remains elevated.
existing_solutions: SchoolStatus (Attend), Panorama, EveryDay Labs, Attendance Works templates, state toolkits, SIS mail-merge.

title: Registering and reporting a Registered Apprenticeship program is slow and paperwork-heavy enough that DOL imposed a 30-day 'shot clock' in 2026
affected_user: Employers and intermediaries sponsoring Registered Apprenticeship programs (especially skilled trades); state apprenticeship agencies; apprentices awaiting registration
job_to_be_done: Get a program's standards approved and registered, then keep apprentice records current in RAPIDS/state systems and file WIPS/PIRL reports
current_process: Sponsor drafts standards (often from DOL templates/National Guideline Standards), submits to the Office of Apprenticeship or State Apprenticeship Agency, negotiates revisions, then enters apprentice data into RAPIDS and periodic federal/state reports.
what_fails: Registration determinations have taken long enough that OA's 2026 Bulletin 2026-35 commits to decisions within 30 days of final signed standards; DOL rulemaking acknowledges a requirement created greater burden than expected on sponsors as they engage with RAPIDS while protecting apprentice confidentiality; 2024 rulemaking cites complaints from would-be sponsors (particularly skilled trades) unable to register in certain states.
failure_frequency: unknown; DOL's own bulletin and rule preambles indicate the problem was common enough to prompt federal action.
cost_of_failure: Delayed program starts and delayed apprentice wage progression; sponsor staff/consultant time; lost state/federal incentives tied to registration. No dollar estimate found.
existing_workaround: Intermediaries and consultants who package standards; vendor sponsor-management software (GoSprout, JobCannon guides); copying National Guideline Standards.
who_pays_today: Sponsors (staff/consultants), DOL/SAA grant programs, intermediaries funded by DOL grants, software vendors.

sources.note: DOL OA bulletin committing to registration determinations within 30 days of final signed standards.
Proposed rule states a requirement caused greater-than-expected burden on sponsors interacting with RAPIDS.
DOL received complaints from potential sponsors, particularly skilled trades, unable to register programs in certain states.
Vendor guide describing RAPIDS/WIPS/PIRL reporting pain for sponsors.

firsthand_evidence: None found directly; DOL rule preambles report receiving sponsor complaints (secondhand institutional record).
key_unknowns: Actual median registration time before/after the shot clock; number of sponsors affected; whether RAPIDS has any API or bulk upload a third party could use; whether sponsors would pay for tooling vs. relying on free intermediaries.
technical_unlock: Standards-drafting templates and apprentice-record management that export to RAPIDS formats; limited by lack of public RAPIDS API.
why_now: DOL 2026 shot-clock bulletin and 2025 deregulatory rulemaking signal active policy change around sponsor burden.
existing_solutions: GoSprout, ApprentiScope, Apprenticeship.gov standards builder, state SAA portals, intermediaries.
